proposals.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon trace Rodney’s early use of Fanon’s analysis of the national bourgeoisie when interpreting Tanzania’s socialist experiment.
proposals.evidence_note: Named scholarly readers Chukwudinma and Kallon 2025 explicitly identify The Pitfalls of National Consciousness as Rodney’s frequently invoked resource during 1969–74 and afterwards. They quote his 1972 accounts of the dependent petty bourgeoisie and intelligentsia’s possible transformation, while distinguishing his terminology from Fanon’s and crediting Cabral for a class-suicide formulation Rodney associated with Fanon. The authors show later revision and continuing debt rather than an unchanging or exclusive lineage. This is their attributed analysis of quoted published and archival Rodney material; the original papers, full lectures and Fanon book remain unread.
primary_locators: 2025 original publisher rendered body: paragraphs beginning Of all Fanon’s writings, The early Rodney subscribed, and In addition, the early Rodney; subsequent post-1974 revision paragraphs. No original print page or complete reference list collated.

proposals.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon identify Rodney’s later disagreements with Fanon over revolutionary organization and the class character of postcolonial African societies.
proposals.evidence_note: The authors’ 2025 original article quotes Rodney’s 1973 Cabral eulogy and 1978 Hamburg distinction between violence itself and its political organization, then traces his post-1974 view of Tanzania’s bureaucracy as a ruling class rooted in production. They describe a move beyond the early model of a dependent stratum that might renounce privilege. Their account expressly calls Rodney’s portrayal of Fanon as an apostle of spontaneity a misreading, since Fanon also demanded organization; it also finds that Rodney retained some Fanonian hopes about guerrilla leadership. The disagreement is Rodney’s interpretation as mediated by these two readers, not a finding that Fanon simply ignored organization or a complete rejection of Fanon. Original eulogy, recordings, research papers and Fanon book unread. The existing James 401 criticism concerns a distinct retrospective assessment of Rodney.
primary_locators: 2025 original publisher body, From spontaneous revolutionary violence to the problem of organisation: paragraphs beginning One would think, A eulogy that Rodney delivered, and Rodney’s misreading; quoted 1978 distinction; later The Rodney of the post-1974 and concluding Rodney and Fanon in dialogue.

proposals.relationship: Harding, Hill and Strickland credit Wallerstein with helping organize Rodney’s lecture and teaching visits while he worked under repression in Guyana.
proposals.evidence_note: The jointly authored introduction, copyright 1981 and reproduced in the actual licensed Verso 2026 preview, names Wallerstein at Binghamton and James Turner at Cornell as especially helpful in organizing opportunities for Rodney to lecture and teach abroad. It explains that these visits sustained contacts and earned money his family needed while he remained in Guyana. Both helpers retain credit. This is their specific retrospective testimony about practical scholarly support, not an inference that Wallerstein supervised Rodney or supplied his dependency theory. The preview ends within Walter’s Legacy and omits the introduction’s endnotes; no complete introduction, original 1981 pagination or full book read.
primary_locators: Joint Harding/Hill/Strickland introduction: paragraph beginning With the help of many persons, immediately following the WPA and research discussion; parenthesis naming James Turner and Immanuel Wallerstein. Actual licensed reflow preview, no original print-page locator.
